auraIntro: Explorer, Pinwheel Galaxy is an immense face-on spiral galaxy containing over 1 trillion stars and 3,000 starbirth regions.
overview: The Pinwheel Galaxy (M101) is a giant face-on spiral galaxy located approximately 25 million light-years away in the constellation Ursa Major.
formation: Formed approximately 13.1 billion years ago, tidal interactions with nearby companion galaxies asymmetricized its outer arms and accelerated starbirth.
structure: A face-on grand spiral galaxy spanning 170,000 light-years—nearly double the size of the Milky Way—with a stellar population of 1 trillion stars.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by Pierre Méchain on March 27, 1781, and cataloged by Charles Messier.
observationTips: Due to its face-on orientation, surface brightness is spread across a large area; requires dark skies to resolve individual spiral arm nodes.
funFacts: Contains over 3,000 giant H II regions where active star formation creates massive newborn star clusters.
Nearly twice the diameter of our Milky Way Galaxy, holding an estimated 1 trillion stars.

cards.title: Arrival: The Colossal Stellar Wheel
cards.subtitle: Messier 101 Overview
cards.body: Welcome to the Pinwheel Galaxy (M101), an enormous face-on spiral galaxy spanning 170,000 light-years across space—nearly twice the diameter of our Milky Way. Located 25 million light-years away in Ursa Major according to NASA's Hubble catalog, M101 provides astronomers an unobstructed top-down view of spiral galaxy structure.

cards.title: Discovery: Pierre Méchain & Messier 101
cards.subtitle: Cataloging the Pinwheel
cards.body: Discovered on March 27, 1781 by French astronomer Pierre Méchain, M101 was among the final deep-sky objects added by Charles Messier to his famous catalog. In the 1850s, Lord Rosse used his 72-inch reflector telescope in Ireland to resolve M101's intricate spiral structure.
bulletPoints: Pierre Méchain discovered M101 in March 1781.
Charles Messier cataloged it as M101 in his original master list.
Lord Rosse recognized its spiral structure using the Leviathan of Parsonstown.

cards.title: Cosmic Story: Asymmetric Arms & 3,000 Nurseries
cards.subtitle: Tidal Disturbances & Extreme Starbirth
cards.body: M101's spiral arms are noticeably off-center and asymmetric. Past gravitational encounters with companion galaxies (NGC 5470, NGC 5474, and NGC 5477) distorted its stellar disk. These tidal forces compressed gas, creating over 3,000 ionized H II starburst regions where massive stars are rapidly forming.
bulletPoints: Asymmetric arm structure caused by gravitational tugs from small companion galaxies.
Hosts over 3,000 giant H II regions where hydrogen gas glows bright pink.
Several H II regions (like NGC 5461 and NGC 5462) are so massive they have their own NGC designations.

cards.title: Deep Insight: Webb Infrared & PAHs Chemistry
cards.subtitle: Infrared Mapping of Interstellar Dust
cards.body: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope observed M101 in infrared light, penetrating interstellar dust clouds. Webb mapped organic molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and fine silicate dust grains, giving scientists unprecedented data on how organic chemistry evolves inside galaxy starbirth zones.
bulletPoints: JWST infrared vision maps warm dust lanes obscured in optical light.
Detects polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) associated with star formation.
Provides precise measurements of gas density and dust grain growth.

cards.title: Cosmic Curiosity: Supernova SN 2023ixf
cards.subtitle: Stellar Cataclysm in May 2023
cards.body: On May 19, 2023, amateur astronomer Koichi Itagaki discovered supernova SN 2023ixf in one of M101's spiral arms. A Type II supernova caused by the collapse of a massive red supergiant star, SN 2023ixf became one of the brightest and closest supernovae observed in over a decade.
bulletPoints: SN 2023ixf exploded in M101 in May 2023, visible with small telescopes.
Progenitor star was identified as a red supergiant ~15-20 times the mass of our Sun.
Allowed multi-observatory study from radio to X-ray wavelengths.
